lead: This unit is about the hardware at the edge of an IoT system: the sensor that measures, the actuator that acts, and the board, radio and battery that tie them into a smart object. After it you can read a sensor datasheet, choose a motor and a radio, size a battery, pick between a microcontroller and a single-board computer, and explain how many nodes form a wireless sensor network and how each thing gets an identity.
about: The unit runs from the two ends of every IoT device to the network they form. 2.1 covers sensors and transducers: the static and dynamic characteristics that decide whether a reading can be trusted, and the resistive, capacitive, inductive, optical and ultrasonic families. 2.2 turns to actuators, mainly BLDC, stepper and servo motors. 2.3 packs a sensor, a processor, a radio, a power unit and an identity into a smart object or sensor node, and 2.4 takes those blocks apart as control units, communication modules and power sources. 2.5 compares microcontrollers such as the ATmega328P with single-board computers such as the Raspberry Pi. 2.6 networks many nodes into a wireless sensor network, and 2.7 gives every object an electronic identity with RFID.

chapters.idea: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, and its characteristics decide how far that signal can be trusted.
chapters.depth: Start with three words: a sensor responds to a physical quantity, a transducer converts one form of energy into another, and a signal conditioner makes the output usable. Classify sensors as active or passive, primary or secondary, analog or digital. Give the mechatronics modular view in one paragraph: sensing module, processing module, actuation module and drive module, joined by signal flow and power flow. Then the static characteristics, each with symbol and unit: range, span, accuracy, precision, resolution, sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, repeatability, drift, dead band, threshold, loading effect. Dynamic characteristics: zero-order, first-order with time constant τ (63.2% of the final value in τ seconds), second-order with natural frequency ωₙ and damping ratio ζ; rise time, settling time, bandwidth. Circuit families: resistive (potentiometer, strain gauge with gauge factor, RTD, thermistor), capacitive (C = εA/d), inductive (LVDT, eddy current), resonant (quartz crystal). Optical: LDR, photodiode, phototransistor, responsivity in A/W. Vision systems, laser sensors, fibre-optic and non-fibre-optic sensing are advanced; only a few universities teach them past the principle. Close with solid-state (Hall, MEMS), piezoelectric and ultrasonic sensors.

figure.aria: A classification tree of sensor families, each branch labelled with the physical quantity it usually measures.

chapters.example: A transmitter gives 4–20 mA for 0–100 °C. (a) Find the span and the sensitivity in mA/°C. (b) What temperature does 12.00 mA show? (c) At 60 °C the rising reading is 13.60 mA and the falling reading is 13.68 mA; find the hysteresis in mA and in °C. Answer: span = 20 − 4 = 16 mA over 100 °C, so sensitivity = 16/100 = 0.16 mA/°C; temperature = (12.00 − 4)/0.16 = 50.0 °C; hysteresis = 13.68 − 13.60 = 0.08 mA = 0.08/0.16 = 0.5 °C.
chapters.trap: Accuracy, precision and resolution are three different things, and a transducer is the converter inside a measuring system, not the whole instrument.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, for where a sensor sits in an IoT device.
chapters.leave: ADC conversion and signal conditioning to 2.4 and 2.5; radio links to 2.6 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: An actuator turns an electrical command into motion or force, and the motor type decides whether that motion is precise, fast or cheap.
chapters.depth: Define an actuator and separate it from a sensor. Group actuators by energy source: electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, thermal, magnetic; give solenoids and relays as simple on-off actuators. Spend most space on the motors the syllabi name. BLDC: permanent-magnet rotor, stator windings, Hall sensors, electronic commutation, six-step versus sinusoidal drive, and why it needs a driver and not just a voltage. Stepper: variable-reluctance and hybrid construction, step angle, holding torque, detent torque, microstepping, open-loop positioning and lost steps. A 1.8° hybrid has 50 rotor teeth, a tooth pitch of 360/50 = 7.2°, and 4 steps per electrical cycle. DC servo and AC servo: closed loop with encoder or resolver, four-quadrant torque-speed, holding position under load. Selection in words: torque at the needed speed, inertia, duty cycle, accuracy, cost, controller. Keep hydraulic and pneumatic valve sizing to one line; only a few universities examine it.

figure.aria: A position control loop: set point, controller, driver, motor and load, with the encoder feeding the measured position back.

chapters.example: A hybrid stepper has a step angle of 1.8° and drives a lead screw of pitch 2 mm. (a) How many steps per revolution? (b) How much linear travel per step? (c) With 1/8 microstepping, what is the resolution in degrees and in micrometres? Answer: (a) 360/1.8 = 200 steps/rev; (b) 2 mm/200 = 0.01 mm = 10 µm per step; (c) 1.8/8 = 0.225° per microstep, and 2000 µm/1600 = 1.25 µm.
chapters.trap: A stepper runs open loop and can lose steps silently, while a servo is closed loop; also a 1.8° step angle is not the microstep resolution.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for the sensor side of the feedback loop.
chapters.leave: PWM generation and driver wiring to 2.4 and Unit 4; control algorithms to a control systems course.

chapters.idea: A smart object is a small package of sensing, computing, communication, power and identity that can report on itself and act.
chapters.depth: Define a smart object and list the five blocks: processing unit, sensing/actuation unit, communication unit, power unit, identification unit. Contrast sensor node (also called a mote), smart object and IoT device in one line each. Sensor node internals: sensing unit with ADC, processing unit with microcontroller and memory, transceiver, power unit, optional location or mobility unit. The awareness–representation–interaction view of smart objects is advanced; two sentences are enough. Communication criteria: range, data rate, duty cycle, latency, reliability, energy per useful bit, topology, cost, licence band. Do one energy budget to show why the sleep current and duty cycle decide battery life, not the peak current. Finish with the node software cycle: sense, convert, compute, transmit, sleep.

figure.aria: The inside of a sensor node: sensor, ADC, microcontroller, transceiver, with the power unit feeding every block and an identity block attached.

chapters.example: A node runs on a 1000 mAh battery of which 80% is usable. It draws 8 mA for 200 ms every 60 s and 3 µA otherwise. Find the average current and the battery life in days. Answer: awake fraction = 0.2/60 = 0.00333; average = 8 × 0.00333 + 0.003 × 0.99667 = 0.02667 + 0.00299 = 0.0297 mA. Life = 800 mAh / 0.0297 mA = 26 975 h ≈ 1124 days ≈ 3.1 years.
chapters.trap: A sensor is one block of a smart object, not a smart object; and battery life follows the average current, so the sleep current and quiescent draw matter as much as the transmit burst.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 and 2.2 for the sensing and actuation blocks.
chapters.leave: Radio standards to Unit 3; the cloud side to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Every IoT device is a control unit, a communication module and a power source built around its sensors, and each part is chosen against the other two.
chapters.depth: Take the smart object apart into buyable parts. Control unit: microcontroller or SoC, clock, memory, GPIO, ADC, PWM, timers, buses (UART, SPI, I²C), and how much compute a node really needs. Communication module: transceiver chip, matching network, antenna, certified module, firmware stack; name the common choices (Wi-Fi, BLE, IEEE 802.15.4/ZigBee, LoRa, NB-IoT, cellular) with typical range and data rate, leaving protocol detail to Unit 3. Power source: mains adaptor, primary cell, Li-ion/LiPo, coin cell, energy harvesting from light, vibration or heat; LDO versus switching regulator, quiescent current, protection, battery gauge. Add the security element and real-time clock as optional blocks. Close with a selection procedure: application → range and data rate → radio → energy per day → battery or harvester → control unit.

figure.aria: A map of five radios placed by range (left to right) and data rate (bottom to top), with the 2.4 GHz band links and the two LPWAN options marked.

chapters.example: A node runs from a 3.7 V, 1200 mAh Li-ion cell. The 3.3 V rail draws 30 mA on average and the regulator is 85% efficient. Find the battery life. What is the life if sleep scheduling brings the average down to 3 mA? Answer: cell energy = 3.7 V × 1.2 Ah = 4.44 Wh. Load power = 3.3 × 0.030 = 99 mW; input power = 99/0.85 = 116.5 mW; life = 4.44/0.1165 = 38.1 h. At 3 mA: load 9.9 mW, input 11.65 mW, life = 4.44/0.01165 = 381 h ≈ 15.9 days.
chapters.trap: Choosing a radio by data rate alone, and mixing mAh (charge) with mA (current) when sizing a battery.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 for the block model of a node.
chapters.leave: Board-level detail to 2.5; protocol stacks to Unit 3; cloud platforms to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A microcontroller gives deterministic control in tiny power, while a single-board computer gives an operating system, memory and connectivity.
chapters.depth: Embedded system definition and the properties that separate it from a PC: fixed function, real-time response, small memory, low power, long life. Block diagram of an embedded board: CPU core, program memory, data memory, timers, interrupt controller, GPIO, ADC, serial buses. Von Neumann versus Harvard, 8/16/32-bit width, clock speed, instructions per second. Compare microcontroller, microprocessor, SoC and single-board computer. Work through two named boards: Arduino Uno (ATmega328P, 16 MHz, 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM, 14 digital I/O, 6 analog inputs, 10-bit ADC, 5 V logic) and Raspberry Pi (ARM Cortex-A, 1 GB or more RAM, Linux, 3.3 V GPIO, no analog input). Mention ESP8266 and ESP32 as microcontrollers with a radio built in. Bare metal versus RTOS versus Linux, and how that choice fixes the response time. End with a one-page rule for choosing.

figure.aria: A choice tree of embedded platforms: microcontrollers on one side and single-board computers on the other, each with two example boards.

chapters.example: An Arduino Uno uses a 10-bit ADC with V_ref = 5.00 V. Find the resolution in mV, the code for 1.20 V, and the input that produces code 512. Answer: resolution = 5.00/2¹⁰ = 5.00/1024 = 4.88 mV per step. Code for 1.20 V = 1.20/0.00488 = 245.7, so 245. Input for code 512 = 512 × 4.88 mV = 2500 mV = 2.50 V.
chapters.trap: Raspberry Pi GPIO has no analog input, so an external ADC is needed; Arduino works at 5 V logic while Pi GPIO is 3.3 V, so level shifting is required.
chapters.leave: Arduino IDE, sketches and Python programming to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A wireless sensor network is many small nodes that sense, cooperate and pass data hop by hop to a sink.
chapters.depth: Define WSN and its elements: nodes, sink or base station, gateway. Topologies: star, tree, mesh; single-hop versus multi-hop. Node architecture in one line, pointing back to 2.3. Protocol stack layers — physical, MAC, routing, transport, application — only at the level of what each layer must do; IEEE 802.15.4, ZigBee and 6LoWPAN detail belongs to Unit 3. MAC idea: duty cycling and contention, and why listening time is the enemy. Routing: flooding, gossiping, LEACH clustering, directed diffusion; only a few universities examine directed diffusion, so keep it short. Coverage, connectivity, localisation and time synchronisation in a line each. Energy: the radio energy model, why two short hops can beat one long hop, and three definitions of network lifetime. Challenges: limited energy, changing topology, fault tolerance, clock drift, security.

figure.aria: A four-node sensor network with a sink: node A can reach the sink directly over 100 m, or through B or C in two 50 m hops.

chapters.example: Use the radio model with E_elec = 50 nJ/bit for the electronics and amplifier ε = 100 pJ/bit/m². Compare the energy per bit for sending directly 100 m with sending over two hops of 50 m. Answer: direct E = 50 nJ + 100 pJ × 100² = 50 nJ + 1000 nJ = 1050 nJ = 1.05 µJ/bit. Per hop of 50 m: 50 nJ + 100 pJ × 2500 = 50 + 250 = 300 nJ; two hops = 600 nJ = 0.6 µJ/bit. Two hops save 0.45 µJ/bit, about 43%.
chapters.trap: A WSN is not a Wi-Fi network: nodes are constrained and multihop. And multihop saves transmit energy but adds latency, routing overhead and more receive energy.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 for node architecture and 2.5 for the microcontroller inside it.
chapters.leave: 802.15.4, ZigBee and 6LoWPAN detail to Unit 3; security to Unit 5; applications to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: RFID gives a thing an electronic identity that a reader can capture without contact or line of sight.
chapters.depth: What identification means for IoT and why a database key needs a reader. RFID parts: tag (chip plus antenna), reader (transmitter, receiver, antenna), middleware. Frequency bands with typical range and one use each: LF 125–134 kHz, HF 13.56 MHz, UHF 860–960 MHz, microwave 2.45 GHz and 5.8 GHz. Passive, semi-passive and active tags; near-field inductive coupling versus far-field backscatter. EPC and EPC Gen 2: the 96-bit code and the singulation idea (slotted ALOHA, binary tree) in two sentences. NFC as HF RFID at 13.56 MHz with a phone. Compare with barcode and QR: no line of sight, many tags at once, rewritable. Other identifiers: IPv6 address, 6LoWPAN, BLE beacons. Close with privacy: hidden tags and tracking of people.

figure.aria: A passive tag inventory: the reader queries, the tag answers with a random number, the reader acknowledges it, the tag sends its 96-bit EPC, and the reader passes it to the server.

chapters.example: A reader at 866 MHz radiates 2 W ERP. A passive tag needs 30 µW at its chip to wake up, and its antenna gain is 2 (about 3 dBi). Find the power reaching the tag at 3 m and the maximum read range in free space. Answer: λ = 300/866 = 0.346 m, so effective aperture A_e = Gλ²/(4π) = 2 × 0.12/12.57 = 0.0191 m². Power density at 3 m: S = 2/(4π × 3²) = 0.0177 W/m². Received power = 0.0177 × 0.0191 = 3.38 × 10⁻⁴ W = 338 µW. Since power falls as 1/d², d_max = 3 × √(338/30) = 3 × 3.36 = 10.1 m.
chapters.trap: A passive tag has no battery, so its read range is set by the power the reader delivers to it; do not quote the backscatter link as if it were the limit. Also keep RFID and NFC in their correct bands.
chapters.prereq: 2.4 for the radio module and power ideas.
chapters.leave: Protocol frames and standards detail to Unit 3; privacy and security law to Unit 5.

links: a measured quantity needs an actuator to act on it
sensor and actuator become blocks of one smart object
node blocks become control unit, radio and power source
the control unit is a microcontroller or a single-board computer
microcontrollers and radios are what a WSN is built from
many sensor nodes networked make a WSN
networked things still need an identity, which RFID supplies
